It seems I'm having trouble getting search results. Let me analyze each option based on my knowledge of analytical chemistry:

A. Karl Fischer titration - This is primarily used for water content determination, not deuterium.

B. NMR spectroscopy with internal standard - Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is highly sensitive to different isotopes. Deuterium (²H) has different nuclear spin properties than regular hydrogen (¹H). NMR spectroscopy with an internal standard of known concentration can be used to quantitatively determine the deuterium content in a deuterated solvent by comparing signal intensities.

C. Gas volumetry - This technique measures gas volume, typically used for gases evolved in chemical reactions, not directly applicable for isotope determination in liquids.

D. Inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) - While this can detect isotopes, it's primarily used for elemental analysis rather than isotope ratio determination, especially for heavier elements.

E. Potentiometry with an ion-selective electrode - This measures ion concentration in solution but isn't specifically designed for isotope discrimination.

Based on my analysis, NMR spectroscopy with an internal standard (option B) is the most appropriate method for determining deuterium content in deuterated solvents. NMR is specifically sensitive to different isotopes and can distinguish between hydrogen and deuterium. Using an internal standard allows for quantitative determination of deuterium content.
